newsitem.title: UK: British MP proposes controversial fox-hunting ban.
newsitem.headline: British MP proposes controversial fox-hunting ban.

text.p: A British Labour member of parliament set the stage on Monday for a bitter clash between the House of Commons and the House of Lords, the unelected upper chamber of parliament, by unveiling a bill to ban fox-hunting.

The new Labour government promised in its manifesto for last month's election to allow a free vote -- letting MPs follow their consciences instead of a party line -- on whether hunting with hounds should be banned.
But Prime Minister Tony Blair had hoped to delay any vote, fearing stubborn resistance from pro-hunting aristocrats in the House of Lords would impede more important legislation.

However, Labour MP Mike Foster, who topped the annual ballot for a slot in the parliamentary timetable to introduce a measure of his choosing, confirmed on Monday that his bill would aim to outlaw hunting of foxes, hares, stags and minks with hounds.
"It's a cruel and barbaric practice that should have ended centuries ago along with cock-fighting, bear-baiting and dog-fighting," Foster told a news conference.

He sidestepped questions as to whether he had come under pressure from the Labour leadership to choose a less controversial bill. The overwhelming pressure, he said, had come from his constituents who want fox-hunting banned.

Even if Foster's bill is backed by a large majority when MPs vote on it on November 28, its fate could depend on the government's willingness to find room in parliament's crowded timetable for it to complete its remaining stages.
Officials refused to make any promises, saying the government would have to take into account its other legislative priorities.

The bill is likely to be deeply unpopular in rural communities. The British Field Sports Society has estimated that outlawing foxhunting would force most of Britain's 300 hunts to close, meaning the loss of as many as 33,000 jobs.
But Foster said only hundreds of jobs would be at risk -- and only if hunts refused to take up the alternative of drag-hunting, in which hounds pursue an artificial scent rather than a fox.
Farmers fear a ban, as well as ending the colourful sight of scarlet-coated riders racing behind a pack of baying hounds, would make it impossible to keep down the fox population.
But animal rights groups, whose protests at hunts lead occasionally to violent clashes, say that foxes could be culled if need be in much more humane ways.
Foster said he was braced for fierce opposition to his bill in the House of Lords, a bastion of the rich landowning classes for whom hunting has been a way of life for centuries.
"If it takes 12 or 18 months, so be it," he said.
